commonMisreadings: Every lever climbs at the same rate, so any man who trains will attract women.
boundaryConditions: The climb is described as uneven and partial; naming it one of the few movable areas is not a promise that any given man moves.

commonMisreadings: Crossing the SMV threshold means women want a man permanently, so he stops filtering altogether.
boundaryConditions: The inversion is a change in who makes offers, not a change in whether the market can move against him again.

commonMisreadings: A man rejected early has weak leverage permanently, so building competence and status changes little.
boundaryConditions: Back-loaded describes a typical shape, not a guarantee; the card's actual claim is about how early rejection should be read.

commonMisreadings: Bitterness is the rational male response once a man sees that women want the strongest offer.
boundaryConditions: Construction is offered as the rational response to being the default offer, which is a claim about strategy rather than about fairness.

commonMisreadings: A woman asking a man to say what he wants will welcome any answer he gives.
boundaryConditions: A flat refusal after an invitation to be direct is read here as the invitation being insincere, not as an obligation to say yes.

commonMisreadings: Wrapping the intention is dishonest, so a man who wants sex should state it bluntly.
boundaryConditions: The card changes the framing and keeps the intent; it is a claim about delivery, not permission to conceal what is wanted.

commonMisreadings: A man who whispers that he wants to make her feel good is hiding the ball.
boundaryConditions: The defence depends on context making the meaning obvious; the same line in an ambiguous setting would be the cop-out the card names.

commonMisreadings: Women complaining that male attention feels transactional on dating apps are inventing the pattern.
boundaryConditions: This card grants the other side's complaint; granting it does not withdraw the punished-directness claim it sits beside.

commonMisreadings: Women reward direct men, so hiding intentions costs a guy attraction on every date.
boundaryConditions: Training is meant in the behavioural sense of what gets rewarded, which is a claim about aggregate response rather than intent.

commonMisreadings: Inviting a woman over for wine works because both sides want the deniability removed.
boundaryConditions: Plausible deniability is described as the mechanism; describing why the move works is not an endorsement of using it to obscure consent.

commonMisreadings: Women who reject blunt men keep their dating pool exactly as wide as before.
boundaryConditions: The filtering is an aggregate effect across many individual choices, so it implies nothing about any one woman's dating pool.

commonMisreadings: Asking where the good men went settles why a woman attracts fewer of the men she wants.
boundaryConditions: The card redirects the question inward; doing so does not establish that the market has stayed the same underneath.

commonMisreadings: Men resent the gap wrongly, since women want honest guys and smooth talkers equally.
boundaryConditions: Explaining where the resentment comes from is not a defence of it; the neighbouring cards argue against letting it curdle.

commonMisreadings: Women want the script they were taught, and they coordinate the mismatch deliberately.
boundaryConditions: Conditioning is the weaker and more defensible claim: shared programming produces a shared pattern without anyone coordinating it.

commonMisreadings: Game became an industry because honest men were already attracting the women they wanted.
boundaryConditions: This explains why the industry grew, which is a different question from whether what it teaches is true or worth learning.

commonMisreadings: Every man learns game eventually, so the honest and direct ones date just as well.
boundaryConditions: Two types is a deliberate simplification of a spectrum; most men sit somewhere between playing fully and refusing entirely.

commonMisreadings: A woman who settles for the honest guy comes to desire him once she commits.
boundaryConditions: The loop is a pattern some men live through, not a law; plenty of honest men never enter it and some settled pairings work.

commonMisreadings: Modern dating rewards effort like a job hunt, so more applications reliably win a partner.
boundaryConditions: The analogy is offered for how the process feels, and it breaks down precisely where volume stops helping.

commonMisreadings: Playing lightly means quitting dating, since low investment and total withdrawal are identical.
boundaryConditions: Low investment lowers the emotional cost and the odds together; it is a way to stay in without grinding, not a strategy for winning.

commonMisreadings: Being yourself and waiting for the right person is the advice that actually finds partners.
boundaryConditions: Calling the slogans a deflection is a claim about why they get repeated, not proof that every pattern they dismiss is real.

commonMisreadings: Being nice is enough on its own, so a woman will want a man who is kind.
boundaryConditions: Both pieces of advice are treated as true but incomplete, which is a repair rather than a rejection of them.

commonMisreadings: People admit plainly that attraction and status drive their dating choices rather than values.
boundaryConditions: This is a claim about what people say in public, not about whether attraction or values actually drives them.

commonMisreadings: Men who analyse dating coldly reach wildly different conclusions, so the patterns are imagined.
boundaryConditions: Convergence among people reasoning the same way is weak evidence on its own; shared premises reach shared conclusions whether or not they hold.

commonMisreadings: Women course-correct early, so most reassess their dating choices well before options thin out.
boundaryConditions: Usually is doing real work in this card; it describes a common trajectory and not an inevitable one.

commonMisreadings: Body positivity changes what men find attractive, so a woman can shift the market by demanding it.
boundaryConditions: Self-acceptance and facing what is changeable are treated as compatible; the target is the version taken far enough to discourage either.

commonMisreadings: Speed-dating research shows looks matter far less to women than to men when they meet face to face.
boundaryConditions: Eastwick & Finkel measured live face-to-face settings; stated preferences and app behaviour are separate measurements that need not agree.

commonMisreadings: Telling a man to find hobbies outside dating is neutral life advice about balance.
boundaryConditions: The reading depends on context — the same advice given unprompted, or to someone genuinely over-invested, can be exactly what it says.

commonMisreadings: Social approval matters little to women, so they break ranks to defend the men they want.
boundaryConditions: The card names a fear of social rejection rather than a character flaw, and the same pressure operates on men in their own groups.

commonMisreadings: Women get cosmetic work because men want it, so male preference drives the fillers and BBLs.
boundaryConditions: Stated male preference for the natural look is survey-grade evidence, and some cosmetic work is done for reasons that have nothing to do with either audience.

commonMisreadings: Today's independence script is freely chosen, unlike the 1950s pressure that pushed women to marry.
boundaryConditions: Both eras carried herd pressure; that leaves open whether either script served the women following it.

commonMisreadings: Noticing that women move together as a group means claiming every woman wants identical things.
boundaryConditions: Group-level tendencies and individual variation are both real; the card rejects the rebuttal, not the variation it points at.

commonMisreadings: Women avoid dangerous edgy men, so the thug-type attraction is a story guys invented.
boundaryConditions: A lot is not most: this describes a visible pattern among some women rather than a general female preference for instability.

commonMisreadings: Learning pickup leaves a man fulfilled once women want him, mask and all.
boundaryConditions: The card grants that game works on the metric of dates and sex; the emptiness it names is a separate cost, not evidence the technique fails.

commonMisreadings: Baseline game means manipulating women, so a socially awkward man can still date well.
boundaryConditions: Game is treated as a scale, so the argument for a required minimum is not an argument for the manipulative end of it.

commonMisreadings: Asking a woman how her day was creates the tension that makes her want him.
boundaryConditions: The example lines are illustrations of a register, not scripts; delivered without the calibration the neighbouring cards demand they land badly.

commonMisreadings: Men born bold attract women, so practice changes little for anyone else.
boundaryConditions: Built rather than born is a claim about the trainable share, and it sits beside cards saying the starting point still differs by temperament.

commonMisreadings: Treating every conversation as a final exam is how a man learns to attract women.
boundaryConditions: The card's own title carries the limit: practice means lowering the stakes for yourself, not misrepresenting your interest to someone else.

commonMisreadings: A woman wants the careful, polite, personality-off version of a man, so restraint reads as authentic.
boundaryConditions: The advice is to stop censoring, which is different from advising the unfiltered version regardless of what it contains.

commonMisreadings: A flat conversation proves a woman rejects him, whatever energy he brought to it.
boundaryConditions: Mirroring explains some flat exchanges and not all of them; raising the energy is a test, not a way to overturn a real no.

commonMisreadings: Refusing to chase works at any level, so an average man can reject women like the top tier.
boundaryConditions: The card conditions the advice on current leverage, which means it changes as leverage does rather than being right or wrong outright.

commonMisreadings: Women are attracted to the real personality underneath the mask, so game sustains a relationship.
boundaryConditions: The dilemma is stated for men whose real presentation gets no traction; it is not a claim that every man faces the same choice.

commonMisreadings: Game is a handful of memorised lines any man can use to attract women.
boundaryConditions: The language analogy cuts both ways: hard to acquire, and genuinely learnable rather than fixed at birth.

commonMisreadings: Dating is fun for everyone, so a man who dislikes the chase enjoys it equally.
boundaryConditions: The same process producing opposite experiences is a claim about temperament, not about who deserves an outcome.

commonMisreadings: Treating a woman you want exactly like a regular person is the route to attraction.
boundaryConditions: Treat her like a woman you are attracted to means adding flirtation, not subtracting the ordinary respect the advice was reaching for.

commonMisreadings: A man should escalate identically whether a woman smiles and touches him or rejects it.
boundaryConditions: Green lights make escalation reasonable rather than guaranteed welcome; they can be withdrawn at any point and the next card covers that.

commonMisreadings: Flirty fantasy texting means a woman wants to come over tonight, so escalate immediately.
boundaryConditions: Fantasy talk is treated as genuine interest that has not yet become a plan, so the card slows the escalation without dismissing the signal.

commonMisreadings: Doubling down on his plan when a woman slows things reads as confident and attractive.
boundaryConditions: Flowing with an off-ramp is about pressure and calibration; it is not advice to abandon direction whenever anything is uncertain.

commonMisreadings: Being a cocky arrogant asshole is real confidence, which is what women want in men.
boundaryConditions: Rejecting the asshole advice is not rejecting boldness; the card asks for playfulness and social awareness held at once.

commonMisreadings: Ambiguous signals are a fair test, and a real man will read what a woman wants.
boundaryConditions: Naming weak signals as a real problem does not make every missed signal her fault; the grey zone still requires a judgement call.

commonMisreadings: A woman saying that's hot is always flirting, whatever her tone and delivery suggest.
boundaryConditions: The card's whole method is that delivery disambiguates, so the phrase carries no fixed meaning on its own.

commonMisreadings: A woman who offers to be his wingwoman and discusses other men wants him romantically.
boundaryConditions: This is one of the few signals the page treats as unambiguous, which is why it is stated flatly rather than hedged.

commonMisreadings: Dating forgives fumbles the way friendships do, so one awkward date costs a man little.
boundaryConditions: Almost zero margin describes the early romantic lane; established relationships and friendships are explicitly the contrast case.

commonMisreadings: A flat thanks to a woman's compliment reads as flirting rather than a closed door.
boundaryConditions: The card explains the freeze as risk management rather than indifference, which is a diagnosis and not a defence of it.

commonMisreadings: A man who was always attractive reads a woman's interest more sharply than a glow-up man.
boundaryConditions: The contrast effect explains a difference in calibration, not a difference in how much attention either man actually receives.

commonMisreadings: A man readier to attract women is one who watched them mock a failed shot.
boundaryConditions: This traces where the over-caution comes from; explaining the origin of the clamp is not the same as excusing staying inside it.

commonMisreadings: Flirting received at work is easy to act on, so a man can reciprocate freely.
boundaryConditions: The bind is specific to being paid to be friendly; away from the register the same signal is readable and actionable.

commonMisreadings: The safest customer-service reply to a woman's opening tells a man exactly what she wants.
boundaryConditions: The cost named here is informational: a flat answer forecloses learning, which is a separate matter from whether it was the polite choice.

commonMisreadings: A woman keeping several male friends for validation wants each of them romantically.
boundaryConditions: The arrangement usually runs without anyone stating it, so naming it describes an exchange rather than alleging a deliberate scheme.

commonMisreadings: The safe guy role is pure loss, and a man learns little about what women want.
boundaryConditions: The card names a genuine gain without disputing the loss; both sit in the same arrangement at the same time.

commonMisreadings: An attractive female friend vouching for a man transfers her status and makes women want him.
boundaryConditions: Usually and can backfire are the card's own hedges; a genuine social introduction is a different move from being vouched for.

commonMisreadings: Looks decide everything, so a man will want a woman whose personality he knows is incompatible.
boundaryConditions: Overriding infatuation requires actually knowing the person, so the mechanism is unavailable for someone he has only looked at.

commonMisreadings: A man who rejects every woman who shows interest is being principled about his standards.
boundaryConditions: The card asks the question rather than answering it; high standards and avoidance can produce the same rejection record.

commonMisreadings: Saying he will know her when he sees her is an open-minded way to choose a partner.
boundaryConditions: The objection is to standards that cannot be checked, not to attraction being partly unpredictable.

commonMisreadings: A man holding out for a pure girl with minimal sexual history will still date widely.
boundaryConditions: The card asks him to price the filter honestly against everything else he wants, which is not an instruction to drop it.

commonMisreadings: A man who avoids the women he wants simply has standards set very high.
boundaryConditions: This is offered as a possibility worth testing against his own pattern, not as a diagnosis that fits every man who holds a high bar.

commonMisreadings: A decent job and gym sessions make a man the catch loyal women want.
boundaryConditions: The card exists to turn the unrealistic-standards charge back on men, so it is a symmetry argument rather than a claim only men do it.

commonMisreadings: Raising his value leaves the entire approach risk on a man, however much women want him.
boundaryConditions: The risk changing hands is a description of high leverage; the neighbouring card warns against adopting the posture before earning it.

commonMisreadings: Staying true to himself guarantees a man finds a partner eventually, so the cost is imaginary.
boundaryConditions: The card states the likely outcome plainly and treats it as a choice being made with open eyes, not a prediction about any individual.

commonMisreadings: A relationship is a necessity like a job, so a man is incomplete until women want him.
boundaryConditions: Calling a relationship optional is aimed at the desperation that makes someone accept anything; it is not an argument against wanting one.

commonMisreadings: Refusing to play the game leaves a man respected by the guys and women he wants.
boundaryConditions: The social cost described is how the choice is read by others, which says nothing about whether the choice itself was right.

commonMisreadings: A principled outsider gets both peace and belonging, so the circle accepts him and the dating works.
boundaryConditions: Usually is the hedge that matters: the trade-off is common rather than universal, and a circle of similar outsiders is the exception.

commonMisreadings: A man who settles for a woman he barely wants takes the painless path.
boundaryConditions: Both paths are stated as painful; the card ranks which pain is bearable rather than claiming one is free.

commonMisreadings: Asking a man about grandchildren when he steps back from dating is pure sincere concern.
boundaryConditions: Often is doing the work here: the same question can be genuine concern, and the card asks him to tell the two apart.

commonMisreadings: Wanting children because it is expected is identical to wanting them with a woman you choose.
boundaryConditions: The test is about the source of the wanting; the card explicitly declines to take a position for or against having children.

commonMisreadings: The dating market rewards integrity, so an honest man is repaid for doing everything right.
boundaryConditions: A market failing to reward integrity is a claim about the market's mechanism, not a claim that integrity has no value.

commonMisreadings: Staying true pays a man internally and externally, so integrity brings the women he wants.
boundaryConditions: The internal reward is real and unmeasurable; naming isolation as its price is what keeps the card from being encouragement.

commonMisreadings: Making peace with dating alone means being happy about it and pretending it stopped hurting.
boundaryConditions: The card defines making peace as living with the situation clear-eyed, and says outright that some men never manage it.

commonMisreadings: Red-pill rage and just-be-yourself comfort are the only two responses available to a man in dating.
boundaryConditions: The third path is described as rare and difficult rather than as the obvious choice everyone should make.

commonMisreadings: Feminism gave women freedoms and left every guardrail on marriage and pairing fully intact.
boundaryConditions: The card states the gains as real before naming the cost, and a trade-off is not a verdict on whether the trade was worth making.

commonMisreadings: The commitment question gets asked equally, so women are asked why they reject good men.
boundaryConditions: This is an observation about which question gets asked in public, not a claim that women avoid commitment more than men do.

commonMisreadings: Young men faced one difficulty at a time, so housing costs and dating pressure arrived separately.
boundaryConditions: The claim is about several pressures coinciding; each strand has its own evidence base and they are not equally well measured.

commonMisreadings: Gen Z men are dating and having sex more than Millennials did at the same age.
boundaryConditions: The sourced part is the sexlessness trend; the wider claim about Gen Z having it worse is an inference drawn on top of it.

commonMisreadings: A man in his thirties who sees the game clearly can still date women his age.
boundaryConditions: This describes a specific cohort's experience of the narrowing window; it is not a claim that a man in his thirties is out of options.

commonMisreadings: Red-pill statistics and warnings empower young men, so knowing the odds improves their dating outcomes.
boundaryConditions: The irony named is that information without agency demoralises; that is a claim about effect, not an argument for withholding the information.

commonMisreadings: A good-looking man struggling in dating proves the market is hopeless for everyone below him.
boundaryConditions: One attractive man's difficulty is a single case that can have its own explanation, which is exactly why it cannot carry the inference.

commonMisreadings: A woman with peak leverage should attract offers, since filtering them matters much less.
boundaryConditions: Peak leverage describes a convergence of youth, beauty, novelty and attention; where it sits varies widely between individuals.

commonMisreadings: A woman wants offers at her highest-attention phase, which is also her wisest phase.
boundaryConditions: Front-loaded is stated about the dating market specifically, and the card says outright that it does not reduce a woman to youth or looks.

commonMisreadings: When high-value men grow scarce, attraction alone is enough for a woman to hold one.
boundaryConditions: The inversion described applies at the top of the market she is competing in, not to the market as a whole.

commonMisreadings: Once a worthy offer appears a woman needs only leverage, so warmth and loyalty attract him later.
boundaryConditions: Two distinct skills are named — filtering while leverage is high and competence once a partner is chosen — and neither substitutes for the other.

commonMisreadings: Calling a woman a pick-me is a real rebuttal to what she noticed about women's dating behaviour.
boundaryConditions: The card objects to the label being used in place of an argument; it does not claim every use of it is social policing.

commonMisreadings: Butterflies for the unavailable guy are a reliability signal, so a woman should want that spark.
boundaryConditions: The card separates the flutter from reliability without claiming the two never coincide; a steady man can also produce it.

commonMisreadings: A woman who circles back to the steady man she passed on will genuinely desire him.
boundaryConditions: The loop describes a common sequence rather than an inevitable one, and the resentment it names lands on both people in it.

commonMisreadings: A woman who leans on male friends for validation is giving them what they want.
boundaryConditions: The arrangement can exist without intent, which is why the card asks for an honest look rather than alleging manipulation.

commonMisreadings: Deciding the standard is unfair changes what men find attractive in a woman's body.
boundaryConditions: Self-acceptance is called healthy in the same breath; the target is using it to avoid what could actually be changed.

commonMisreadings: Blaming men is more useful for a woman than asking which men still want her.
boundaryConditions: Turning the question inward is offered as the more useful move, not as proof that the market side of the complaint is empty.

commonMisreadings: Performing the nicer story is how a woman names what actually drives which men she wants.
boundaryConditions: Being driven by attraction and status is treated as ordinary rather than shameful; the card objects to concealing it, not to having it.

commonMisreadings: Men avoid commitment, so a woman waiting to see if someone better wants her is strung along.
boundaryConditions: The card turns a script around; men avoiding commitment is not denied, only its assumed monopoly on the pattern.

commonMisreadings: Waiting until her mid-thirties to reassess leaves a woman the same room to choose well.
boundaryConditions: Reassessing early is advice about preserving choice, and it assumes the wall is a slope rather than the cliff the discourse describes.

commonMisreadings: A shy woman gives a man she wants exactly the same low effort as anyone else.
boundaryConditions: Usually is the hedge: genuine anxiety or an unsafe context can suppress the effort a woman would otherwise show.

commonMisreadings: Every woman on the apps is delusional and entitled, and each of them wants an impossible man.
boundaryConditions: This card exists to bound the rest of the page; conceding the other side's difficulty does not retract the patterns named elsewhere.

commonMisreadings: The frustration is that a woman wants a tall guy with money, rather than her dishonesty about it.
boundaryConditions: Standards are treated as legitimate whatever their content, so the complaint is about accuracy of description and nothing else.

commonMisreadings: The high-school dynamic ends after graduation, so charisma stops deciding who gets chosen in dating.
boundaryConditions: The continuity claim is about who gets selected; adult markets add money, status and timing that high school did not have.

commonMisreadings: A dry low-effort texter turns warm in person, so texting predicts little about dating.
boundaryConditions: Usually a decent preview is a screening heuristic, and the mirroring card next to it names the main way it misfires.

commonMisreadings: A woman who retreats to polite after a flat reply simply stopped wanting him.
boundaryConditions: The standoff is constructed so that neither party is at fault, which is what distinguishes it from genuine disinterest.

commonMisreadings: Most people are above average, so anyone can find the partners they want.
boundaryConditions: The arithmetic constrains how many people clear several bars at once; it says nothing about whether any particular pairing is available.

commonMisreadings: How much a person believes they bring sets their dating value, whatever the market returns.
boundaryConditions: Market response is feedback about a tier and a strategy, not a measure of a person's worth or a fixed ceiling.

commonMisreadings: Waiting for an upgraded self before dating is always the disciplined choice, whatever the delay costs.
boundaryConditions: The card grants that not locking in at a low point has real logic; the trap is the version with no end condition.

commonMisreadings: An agreeable yes to dating signals real interest as reliably as an enthusiastic one.
boundaryConditions: This is about reading enthusiasm accurately; a hesitant yes is still a yes, and the card is not a rule about who may accept.

commonMisreadings: Grinding on yourself first is the right answer at every age, whatever runway remains for dating.
boundaryConditions: The answer is conditioned on remaining runway, which means it is a scheduling judgement rather than a fixed rule either way.

commonMisreadings: Calling someone an incel or a pick-me answers whether their claim about dating is true.
boundaryConditions: Naming the fallacy establishes that the label settles nothing; it does not establish that the underlying claim is correct.

commonMisreadings: Feminism alone explains dating's dysfunction, so apps and social media changed little for anyone.
boundaryConditions: Several threads are named as simultaneous causes, and the card does not weigh them against each other.

commonMisreadings: Men and women read friendliness equally well, so nobody over-reads warmth as romantic interest.
boundaryConditions: Sexual overperception bias is an average difference between groups, so it predicts nothing about a specific reading being wrong.

commonMisreadings: Cold approaching at volume is cheap, so more approaches make more women want an average man.
boundaryConditions: The tax is highest where the same people recur — a gym, a campus, a neighbourhood — and lower in genuinely anonymous settings.

commonMisreadings: Shaming men who date abroad or opt out addresses what made the local market bad.
boundaryConditions: The shop analogy is about which question gets asked; it is not a claim that every exit is a reasoned response to prices.

commonMisreadings: Social environment changes little, so time around socially skilled people leaves a man's dating unchanged.
boundaryConditions: Absorbing calibration by proximity assumes he is actually in the room and participating; the next card is about why that is the hard part.

commonMisreadings: Joining a club is enough to meet the partners a quiet man wants.
boundaryConditions: The mechanism specified is repetition with the same faces plus engagement, which is why attendance alone is the failure mode named.

commonMisreadings: Forcing yourself into a social hobby you dislike reliably works for meeting partners as an introvert.
boundaryConditions: The bind is real for people whose genuine interests are solitary; it is not a claim that introverts cannot build a social life.

commonMisreadings: General meetup groups are full of single people your age looking to date, so attend them.
boundaryConditions: The objection is about the composition of general-interest groups, so a group selected for age and intent is a different case.

commonMisreadings: Meeting partners feels hard for personal reasons, since the casual third spaces are still thriving.
boundaryConditions: Naming a structural cause removes blame without removing the need to act inside the environment as it now is.

commonMisreadings: A shy person who barely dates can still marry, which proves the path is repeatable.
boundaryConditions: The card's point is that a single lucky sequence is not a method; it does not claim such outcomes are impossible.

commonMisreadings: The dating environment is rigged against introverts, so extroverts gained their edge only recently.
boundaryConditions: Calling the extrovert advantage long-standing rejects the conspiracy framing without claiming the current environment is unchanged.

commonMisreadings: Being quiet is what stops a person finding partners, connected or otherwise.
boundaryConditions: The card separates quiet from socially anxious and disconnected, which is a claim about which trait is load-bearing.

commonMisreadings: Dumb-luck stories are a strategy, so a man who keeps going will meet the partner he wants.
boundaryConditions: Calling these stories lottery tickets is about their usefulness as a plan, not a denial that they happened.

commonMisreadings: Asking fast on dating apps selects for people specifically interested in you.
boundaryConditions: The trade named is more meetings of lower average quality, so which side of it is better depends on what is being optimised.

commonMisreadings: Whether the wild card arrives is knowable, so a man can say confidently that dating ends here.
boundaryConditions: The card refuses both confident answers; sitting in the uncertainty is presented as accurate rather than as comforting.

commonMisreadings: A man regrets that women wanted him little, rather than the clear chances he missed.
boundaryConditions: Ranking fumbled chances as the heavier regret is a claim about how it lands, and the next card is the counterweight to it.

commonMisreadings: Freezing when the moment came proves a man is permanently broken for dating rather than untrained.
boundaryConditions: The frame reinterprets past freezing as missing skill; it does not promise the skill has since been acquired.

commonMisreadings: High school and college were as hard for meeting partners as adult life is now.
boundaryConditions: Easy mode refers to the density of same-age contact, not to the outcomes being easy for everyone inside it.

commonMisreadings: Focusing entirely on school and grades leaves a person's dating development fully intact.
boundaryConditions: The advice is called half-true rather than false; the omission is what the card is about.

commonMisreadings: Tracing the exact causes always lightens the weight for a man analysing his dating history.
boundaryConditions: The card raises the question of whether the dissection helps and leaves it genuinely open.

commonMisreadings: Seeing his situation with total clarity means a man will change how he approaches dating.
boundaryConditions: Clarity without change is described as rare rather than admirable; the card names the posture without recommending it.

commonMisreadings: Asking the other side to change is what finally moves dating, so women and men should wait.
boundaryConditions: The symmetry argument says why nothing moves; it does not establish that both sides carry equal responsibility for the situation.

commonMisreadings: Heteropessimists have actually stopped dating men, so the despair predicts who leaves the market.
boundaryConditions: Performed despair and an actual exit are separate measurements, and most speakers produce only the first.
pressureTests: Would this speaker's dating behaviour over the next year differ from someone who never said any of it?

commonMisreadings: Women consciously agreed among themselves on the terms men date under.
boundaryConditions: A default favouring one side is compatible with nobody having chosen it, and with individual women resenting it.
pressureTests: What observation would count against the frame instead of counting as one more instance of it?

commonMisreadings: Men who date now behave identically to the women they pursue.
boundaryConditions: How men get portrayed in media and how boys get taught are separate measurements, and they often disagree.
pressureTests: Which institution, which decade, which outcome — and what would the correct amount of change have looked like?

commonMisreadings: A looks rating drifts freely, so any partner will eventually find you attractive.
boundaryConditions: The band bounds how far perception travels; where the first rating came from is a separate question.
pressureTests: Is the lift inside one observer's band, or is it a fresh rating by a different observer?

commonMisreadings: A top-rated woman dates a partner rated exactly as high as herself.
boundaryConditions: The curve describes couples that already formed, so it cannot be read as who pairs at all.
pressureTests: Is the number an average partner or a typical one, and how wide is the spread around it?

commonMisreadings: A woman's option pool is the set of men she will actually date and keep.
boundaryConditions: Reach into a partner tier and conversion into a couple are separate measurements on the same ladder.
pressureTests: Is this access to a tier, or an outcome recorded with one?
